period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 00min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.85): recite the poem aloud with teacher.
Let us discuss (p.87): match each stanza to its main idea.

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem: First Reading and Stanza Walk

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the poem aloud, stanza by stanza, with students following in their textbooks. Students echo each stanza softly after the teacher to settle the rhythm and rhyme.

Students recite the poem together with the teacher, keeping the song-like quality. The teacher pauses after each stanza to invite one student to say — in a single phrase — what world the bird sees at that point.

The teacher presents the six main-idea sentences from “Let us discuss” (p.87) on the board. Students work in pairs to match each of the four stanzas to its main idea, identifying the two extra sentences and explaining briefly why those do not fit.
Pairs share their matches aloud; the class agrees on the correct four and discusses why “the bird becomes blind due to leaves” and “the bird is unhappy with the straw nest” are the distractors.

periods.teacher_notes: The four-stanza arc — egg, nest, tree, open sky — maps neatly onto four stages of growing up; drawing this out verbally helps students hold the whole poem before they engage with its details. A common pitfall is treating “I have been very blind” as a complaint rather than a moment of humble self-realisation; the poem’s tone is wonder, not regret. Students who find matching difficult may be guided to underline the concrete noun in each stanza (shell, straw, leaves, world) as a quick anchor.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.88): extract questions on the nest stanza.
Let us discuss (p.88): true or false — two statements.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Extract Questions and True/False

time_bands.activity: Students open their textbooks and re-read the second stanza silently. The teacher asks: “What two things does the bird compare its whole world to in this stanza?” to activate close attention before the extract questions.

The teacher leads the class through the extract questions on the nest stanza (“Let us discuss,” p.88): who lived with the bird, why the bird thought the world was made of straw, and which word signals warmth and comfort. Students first write answers individually, then share with a partner before a brief whole-class discussion.

The class tackles the true/false statements (p.88): “The bird changed its house two times” and “The neighbours tell the bird about the world.” Students write their verdicts and one-sentence justifications; the teacher invites two students to read their justifications and the class refines the answers together.

periods.teacher_notes: Having matched stanzas to main ideas in the earlier reading, students now zoom into language detail. A frequent error is answering “the bird changed its house two times” as True by counting egg and nest as two moves and forgetting the third move to the open sky; guide students to count carefully by re-reading all four stanzas. The homework extract (the leaves stanza) asks students to practise independently the same close-reading method used in class today.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.88): extract questions on the leaves stanza — answer in writing.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.88): why did the bird think its first world was small, round and blue?
Let us think and reflect (p.89): what quality did the bird say it had when it flew away?
Let us think and reflect (p.89): who do you think were the bird’s neighbours? Discuss.

periods.activity_title: Discussion and Reflection: The Adult Bird’s Wisdom

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the first and fourth stanzas aloud. Students are asked to think quietly about why the bird’s descriptions of the world changed so dramatically from one stage to the next before sharing their ideas.

The class discusses the reflection question (p.88): why the baby bird thought its first world was small, round, and blue. Students are guided to connect the egg’s physical shape and colour to the bird’s limited perspective inside it.

Students address the question about the quality the bird claims when flying away (p.89). After individual writing, the teacher draws out the phrase “fit for grown-up labours” and asks what kind of quality or readiness that suggests.

A paired discussion on who the bird’s neighbours might be (p.89) and why the neighbours also do not know how the world is made. The teacher invites two or three students to share their reasoning, highlighting the poem’s message of shared wonder.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s central wisdom is that not knowing — and saying so honestly — is itself a kind of maturity; help students articulate this rather than treating the final stanza as a confession of ignorance. A common pitfall is reading “fit for grown-up labours” as purely physical flight rather than as a metaphor for adult readiness and responsibility. The discussion about neighbours is deliberately open: accept answers naming other birds, animals, or people, as long as students support their view with lines from the poem.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.90): fill in missing words while listening to the Paro poem.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Paro the Parrot: Fill in the Missing Words
materials: Gapped poem on board or as handout

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces Paro the parrot briefly — where parrots live, what they look like — to set the scene. Students are given the gapped poem on the board or as a handout and told to keep pens ready before the first reading.

The teacher reads the Paro poem (p.102) aloud at a natural pace while students listen without writing. Students then hear a second reading, this time filling in the missing words in the gaps as they listen.

The teacher reads the poem a third time; students check and correct their answers. Volunteers share their answers for each gap and the class agrees on the correct words by listening once more to the relevant lines.

The teacher asks students to compare the Paro poem’s world — skies, trees, breeze — with the world the bird in the main poem perceives at different stages. Students share one observation aloud as a brief oral exit response.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript for this activity is the eight-line Paro poem (p.102); every missing word is directly recoverable from that text, so three readings are sufficient. A common pitfall is students guessing from surrounding context rather than listening carefully to the precise word; encourage them to leave a gap blank on the first pass rather than guess incorrectly and then struggle to revise. The comparison at the close is informal and unscored — its purpose is to keep the poem’s themes alive.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.90): present in first person which bird you would like to be.

periods.activity_title: I Am a Bird: First-Person Oral Presentation

time_bands.activity: The teacher models the task using the five prompt points — identity, appearance, home, daily routine, message to humans — speaking for about one minute as an example bird. Students note how each prompt leads into the next.

Students choose their bird and draft brief notes for each of the five prompt points. The teacher circulates to help with vocabulary — colour words, habitat nouns — and ensures every student has something to say for each point.

Students present their bird speech one by one or in a quick round — aiming for about one minute each. Listeners are asked to hold one question or observation to share after each presentation, keeping the audience engaged.

The teacher invites the class to vote on the most surprising “message to humans” heard. Two or three students read their message aloud again, and the class reflects briefly on what birds might genuinely need from people.

periods.teacher_notes: The five scaffold points are a support structure, not a script; encourage students to vary sentence openers rather than repeat “I am…” for every line. A common pitfall is students spending most of their time on appearance and rushing the message section, which is the richest point thematically; alert them during the note-making phase to plan at least two sentences for the message. Students who are hesitant to speak aloud may be paired first for a quieter rehearsal before the whole-class round.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.91): five sentences each on how the world looks to a baby and to a fish.

periods.activity_title: Writing Perspectives: How the World Looks to a Baby and a Fish

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the model paragraph (p.91) aloud and asks students to identify the perspective device used — the narrator speaking as the bird. The class briefly discusses what a baby sees, hears, and feels before writing begins.

A quick paired oral discussion: what would a fish’s world look, sound, and smell like? The teacher captures three or four student ideas on the board as a word bank — blue, silent, wet, wavering light, cool — to support writers who need it.
Students write five sentences describing the world from a baby’s perspective in their notebooks. The teacher circulates, prompting for sensory detail and first-person voice where needed.
Students write five sentences for the fish’s perspective. The teacher encourages them to use the word bank on the board and to vary their sentence starters beyond “I see…”
Two or three volunteers read one sentence from each piece aloud. The class responds with a thumbs-up gesture if the sentence convincingly captures that creature’s viewpoint.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task directly extends the poem’s central idea — that the world looks different depending on where you stand — so the teacher should keep the connection explicit during the opening discussion. A common pitfall is students writing descriptively about babies or fish from the outside (“a baby has small hands”) rather than from the inside (“everything looks giant and blurry to me”); the model paragraph on p.91 demonstrates the inside-voice approach and should be re-read if students drift. Both pieces are drafted and reviewed within this sitting so neither depends on a future sitting to close.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.89): complete rhyming-words table for all four stanzas and complete the new stanza.

periods.activity_title: Rhyming Words and Describing Words from the Poem

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the four pairs of rhyming words from the poem — well/shell, other/mother, find/blind, labours/neighbours — and asks students to clap on each rhyming syllable. The class identifies what the words have in common at the end.

Students complete the rhyming-words table for all four stanzas (p.89), adding the words given and then two new rhyming words of their own for each row. Pairs compare their additions and challenge any word that does not rhyme correctly.

The class works on completing the new stanza (p.89) with rhyming words at the end of each line — “know” and “best.” Students then compose one additional couplet of their own using a rhyming pair from the table they built.
Four or five students read their completed new stanzas aloud. The teacher notes on the board any creative rhyming pairs the class invented, celebrating the variety.

periods.teacher_notes: Rhyme in this poem is not merely decorative — the well/shell and other/mother pairs reinforce the cosy, contained feelings of each stage; this connection is worth a brief mention before the table work. A common pitfall is students adding near-rhymes or slant rhymes (e.g., “blind / mind” is fine, but “blind / behind” may need checking); accept slant rhymes with a note that poets use them deliberately. The homework task on describing words (p.90) gives students independent practice with adjective use and is self-contained.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.90): use describing words to write six sentences about the birdhouse picture.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.87): match each picture (egg, nest, branch, flying) to the correct poem line.
Let us discuss (p.87): fill in crossword-style answers from the poem.

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays or describes the four pictures from p.87 one by one — egg, nest with mother, bird on branch among leaves, bird flying away. Students call out which stanza each image belongs to before the written task begins.

Students open to p.87 and write the matching line from the poem next to each picture, working individually. The teacher circulates, asking students to point to the exact line in the poem text, not just recall it from memory.

The word-hunt challenge (p.87): students find the poem word that fits each clue — shape (R–O–U–N–D), nest material (S–T–R–A–W), what the bird saw outside (L–E–A–V–E–S), what it did at the end (F–L–E–W). Students work in pairs and check each answer against the poem.

Quick whole-class check: one pair reads each answer and the letter pattern. The teacher invites students to say which stanza and line each word comes from, reinforcing the poem’s structure one more time.

periods.teacher_notes: These tasks return students to the poem’s text at a finer grain than stanza-level matching, helping them locate specific words and lines with precision. A common pitfall with the word-hunt is students completing the blanks from memory rather than checking the poem; insisting they point to the line in the book makes the reading practice genuine. This unit’s materials are entirely self-contained — only the textbook is needed.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.91): list home materials; discuss why homes are not made of straw; describe your ideal home.

periods.activity_title: Homes and Materials: From Shell to Brick

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the “Let us explore” prompt (p.91) aloud. Students think quietly for a moment about the bird’s three homes — shell, straw nest, open sky — before the teacher asks: “What is your home made of?” Students call out materials they know.

Students make a written list of all the materials their own home is made of (p.91). In pairs, they compare lists and identify any materials the other had not thought of. A brief whole-class share builds a board list of common materials.

Class discussion on two questions: why our homes are not made of straw, and what home a student would design if free to choose any materials. The teacher prompts thinking about weather, safety, cost, and environment.

Students discuss the difference between a home and a house (p.91) in pairs, then share one-sentence ideas with the class. The teacher draws out that a house is a structure while a home is a feeling — connecting back to the poem’s warm nest stanza.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s image of the straw nest as the bird’s entire world is a natural springboard for this interdisciplinary conversation about shelter, materials, and belonging. A common pitfall is the discussion staying abstract; ground it by asking students to name one specific material from their own home and one reason it was chosen over another option. The distinction between house and home is genuinely philosophical — students often arrive at the insight that love and family are the materials that make a house a home.

items.source_lo: Student identifies main ideas and key details in a poem using structured discussion and textual evidence as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-stanza bird poem; egg, nest, leaves, open sky; main-idea matching; true/false; stanza extract questions.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 85 beginning “I lived first in a little house.” In the first stanza the bird describes its world as small, round, and pale blue. Which of the following best explains why the bird perceived its world this way?

options.label: A
options.text: The bird had flown very high and looked down at the round earth below.

options.label: B
options.text: The bird had never left the tree and could only see the sky above.

options.label: C
options.text: The bird was still inside the egg, so its entire world was the shell around it.

options.label: D
options.text: The bird’s mother had painted the nest pale blue to keep it warm.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student is confusing the tree stage (third stanza) with the egg stage.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a detail not present in the poem; student may be guessing rather than reading.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the bird’s grown-up flight in the fourth stanza with the first-stanza perspective.

items.source_lo: Student identifies main ideas and key details in a poem using structured discussion and textual evidence as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-stanza bird poem; egg, nest, leaves, open sky; main-idea matching; true/false; stanza extract questions.
items.item_stem: By the end of the poem the adult bird says it does not know how the world is made, and neither do its neighbours. What does this final admission reveal about what the bird has learned through its journey from egg to open sky? Support your answer with at least one detail from the poem.

expected_elements: Acknowledges that not knowing is itself a form of wisdom.
References the bird’s stages — shell, nest, leaves — as each being incomplete.
Notes that neighbours share the same wonder, showing the feeling is universal.
Uses at least one phrase or image from the poem as evidence.

items.item_stem: After listening to the poem about Paro the parrot, answer the following question in one or two sentences: What two kinds of things does Paro promise to show the listener on their journey through the skies?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Paro promises to take the listener to places old and places new, and to show them many new stories among the trees where the breeze is light.

items.source_context: First-person bird identity speech; appearance, habitat, daily routine, message to humans; five prompt points.
items.item_stem: Choose a bird you find interesting. Speak for about one minute in the first person as that bird. Tell your classmates your name, what you look like, and where you live.

expected_elements: Names the bird and uses “I am” to establish first-person voice.
Describes at least two physical features using colour or size words.
Names a specific habitat with one locating detail.
Speaks clearly enough to be understood by classmates.

items.source_lo: Student delivers a structured first-person oral presentation using guided prompts as the vehicle.
items.source_context: First-person bird identity speech; appearance, habitat, daily routine, message to humans; five prompt points.
items.item_stem: Still speaking as your chosen bird, share your message for humans. Give at least one reason why you feel this way, and respond to a classmate’s message in one sentence.

expected_elements: States a clear message to humans with a stated reason.
Uses opinion language such as “I want” or “I believe.”
Responds meaningfully to a classmate’s point in one sentence.
Maintains the first-person bird voice throughout.

items.source_lo: Student writes in a first-person perspective voice using a model and guided prompts as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five sentences each: how the world looks to a baby and to a fish; inside-voice perspective writing.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are a newborn baby. Write five sentences describing how the world looks, sounds, and feels to you. Use “I” as the narrator and include at least one sensory detail in each sentence.

expected_elements: Five sentences written consistently in first-person voice.
At least one sentence uses a sensory detail (sight, sound, touch, or smell).
Describes the world from inside the baby’s limited perspective, not from outside.
Uses simple, clear sentence structures appropriate to Grade VI.

items.source_lo: Student writes in a first-person perspective voice using a model and guided prompts as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five sentences each: how the world looks to a baby and to a fish; inside-voice perspective writing.
items.item_stem: Think about the poem’s bird, who believed the whole world was made of straw because that was all it could see. Now imagine you are a fish. Write a short paragraph (five to seven sentences) describing your underwater world. Explain one thing you cannot see or understand from inside the water, just as the bird could not see beyond the nest.

expected_elements: Writes from inside the fish’s perspective using first-person voice.
Includes vivid detail about the underwater world (light, water, movement).
Identifies one limitation of the fish’s viewpoint, echoing the poem’s theme.
Connects the fish’s limited view to the bird’s experience, explicitly or implicitly.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and generates rhyming word patterns within a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rhyming pairs from four stanzas: well/shell, other/mother, find/blind, labours/neighbours; new stanza completion.
items.item_stem: The poet of “What a Bird Thought” uses end-rhyme to give the poem a gentle, song-like feel. Look at the rhyming pair “labours / neighbours” in the fourth stanza. In one or two sentences, explain what this rhyme adds to the meaning of the stanza, and then write one new rhyming couplet of your own that captures the idea of the adult bird’s wonder at the vast world.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The rhyme of “labours” and “neighbours” links the bird’s own work in the world with the shared wonder of those around it, suggesting that not knowing is a communal experience. Accept any original couplet where the final words rhyme and the idea of wonder or unknowing is present.

items.source_lo: Student connects a poem’s themes to real-world inquiry about materials, shelter, and community using interdisciplinary discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Home materials list; why homes are not made of straw; ideal home description; home versus house distinction; bird nests; workers’ table.
items.item_stem: The bird in the poem lived in three kinds of homes — a shell, a straw nest, and eventually the open sky. Think about the materials that make up your own home. Write a list of at least five materials you can identify in your home and explain in two sentences why human homes need stronger materials than a bird’s straw nest.

expected_elements: Lists at least five identifiable materials (brick, cement, glass, wood, steel, etc.).
Gives a reason linked to human needs — weather, safety, durability, or size.
Connects the answer back to the poem’s contrast between bird shelter and human shelter.
Writes in complete sentences with reasonable accuracy.
